# Preface {.unnumbered}

## The whole model in two minutes

**Q-CRAFT, the Quantitative Climate Risk Assessment Fiscal Tool, is how the IMF Fiscal Affairs Department projects public finances under climate warming.** It takes a country's published macroeconomic and fiscal data, adds assumptions about demography, productivity, prices and fiscal policy, and projects the [debt-to-GDP ratio](glossary.qmd#gloss-debt-to-gdp-ratio) to 2099 under a baseline and [six warming scenarios](glossary.qmd#gloss-climate-scenarios).

**Underneath sits one equation fed by three numbers.** Each year, the [debt dynamics equation](glossary.qmd#gloss-debt-dynamics-equation) takes last year's debt ratio, grows it by the interest rate, shrinks it by economic growth, and subtracts the primary balance. Warming reaches the projection through two of those numbers, by two named channels. Hotter years drag on productivity, so growth slows. Spending stays rigid while the tax base slows with it, so the primary balance weakens. Each year's dent is small, and the model's subject is what seventy years of small dents compound into.

{{< include figures/_preface-elevator.qmd >}}

**That design buys coverage and speed.** The tool runs on already-published data: the IMF's [WEO](glossary.qmd#gloss-weo) macro series, the UN's population projections, and a short list of choices you set. It needs no bespoke country dataset, no new survey and no waiting for a mission, so it runs for most of the world (the climate estimates cover 171 economies), and a team can have a first pass by week's end.

**The same design keeps the model to one slice of climate change, so read the results as a lower bound, not a central estimate.** The scenarios carry a single channel, the slow effect of rising temperature on productivity. They exclude tipping points, nonlinearities, natural disasters, sea-level rise, the public spending adaptation takes, and whatever channel is specific to your own country ([User Guide, pp. 5-6](references.qmd#src-user-guide)). This is the looking-under-the-streetlight trade, made with open eyes: the model looks where the light is because the lit ground is what nearly every country has published. What the beam misses is left out of the number, not out of the world. @sec-m5 sets out the exclusions with the sources.

**A tool that runs anywhere on published data cannot carry the channel only your country has.** The strengths and limitations follow from that one design choice. This guide teaches what the tool does, why it exists, and what it leaves out. It is the first in a series asking those same three questions of the models behind sovereign climate-fiscal analysis.

## The results reach published fiscal-risk documents

**The Fiscal Affairs Department built Q-CRAFT for its own climate technical assistance, and finance ministries carry the results into fiscal-risk documents they already publish.** The cycle has run end to end in print: Uganda's Fiscal Risk Statement for FY 2024/25 has a chapter on climate fiscal risks whose figures are sourced to "QCRAFT (2023)", tracing back to a five-day workshop written up as *Uganda: PFM Climate Assessment* [(IMF, 2024)](references.qmd#src-imf-2024-uganda). The course moves country by country: Kenya, Thailand and Ethiopia carry teaching examples, and the capstone runs on your own country.

::: {.callout-note}
## This is not an IMF product
Q-CRAFT Explorer and this course are an independent project by [Teal Insights](https://tealinsights.com) and [NatureFinance](https://naturefinance.net). Neither is an official IMF product and neither carries IMF endorsement. Both are meant to be complementary to the IMF's own training materials and to the Q-CRAFT User Guide [(Tim and Rahman, 2024)](references.qmd#src-user-guide), which remain the authoritative references. Where this guide explains a concept it cites the User Guide section behind it, so you can always check the teaching against the source.
:::

## The workbook and the Explorer run the same model

**This course teaches you to run Q-CRAFT both ways: in the official IMF Excel workbook the Fund publishes on its website, and in Q-CRAFT Explorer, an open-source web tool running the same model.** The modules teach on the Explorer. The appendix [Running the official workbook](appendix-workbook.qmd) is the quick orientation to operating the workbook, and the IMF's User Guide remains its official manual.

::: {.qc-shot layout-ncol="2"}
![The official workbook's Dashboard, Uganda selected. [Download it from the IMF](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/topics/fiscal/fiscal-risks/tool/qcraft-toolv10.xlsx).](figures/screenshots/workbook-dashboard.png)

![The same run in Q-CRAFT Explorer. [Open it in your browser](https://teal-insights.github.io/QCraft-App/explorer/).](figures/screenshots/explorer-analysis.png)
:::

**Teal Insights and NatureFinance build the Explorer, its code permissively licensed open source: free to use, copy and improve (the MIT license).** The economics is the IMF's on either surface. The interface, the automatic data loading and the record of what you assumed are ours. Under the interface sits a calculation engine that is its own open-source package, separate enough that a ministry can run the whole tool on its own machines, and checked against the workbook cell by cell, with baseline parity exact for 147 of 147 tested countries and climate-scenario parity confirmed for ratio metrics only. @sec-m1 sets out what that claim covers and what it does not.

**The workbook is where Q-CRAFT lives officially, and Excel is a deliberate choice.** Every finance ministry has Excel, staff already know it, and a Fund tool must run in nearly two hundred countries without assuming data or infrastructure that may not be there. Q-CRAFT is designed simple so it runs pretty much anywhere.

**The Explorer runs that same economics on the web, built so your time goes on the analysis rather than on moving numbers by hand.** In practice:

1. **Up-to-date data.** A posted workbook ships with the WEO vintage it was built on, and that vintage ages between releases. We keep the Explorer's bundled data current.
2. **Guidance where you need it.** Help for choosing a parameter sits beside the parameter, at the moment of choosing. In a deadline week, that is the moment the help gets read.
3. **Fewer steps between the question and the chart.** The data is already loaded and the scenarios already drawn, so more of the hour goes on the policy thinking.
4. **The export packet.** Assumptions, written remarks on them and presentation-ready output come out together, so less of the write-up gets copied by hand.

**@sec-m1 argues these four advantages in full.** After that the course mostly stops arguing them and shows them, one at a time, in the flow of the work.

## The questions it answers

**Q-CRAFT answers a narrow set of questions, each by comparing two runs of the same model.** Run the projection with no climate damage and you have the baseline. Switch one warming scenario on and run it again. The gap between the two paths, read at the year you care about, is the answer.

{{< include figures/_preface-questions.qmd >}}

**None of the four is a forecast.** Each is a difference between two projections built on assumptions you chose, which is why the assumptions are worth arguing about and worth writing down.

## Who this is for

**This course is designed for intelligent, busy people who must run this class of fiscal projection tool, teach it, or read its output.** Ministry of finance economists are its primary readers: they run the tool, then defend the numbers to the officials who sign them off. It equally serves IFI and technical assistance staff who build capacity around tools like this one, and researchers and analysts who read the output and must decide what it lets them claim.

## What you will be able to do

**The course sets three objectives and weights them equally:**

1. **Run the tool, on both surfaces.** Select a country, set the parameters, read the charts and export the results, in the IMF workbook and in the Explorer.
2. **Understand what you are doing when you run it.** Trace the one equation and its three inputs, and see which of your assumptions is moving the answer.
3. **Interpret the output appropriately.** Say what a result supports and what it does not, with its strengths and its limits attached.

**The first objective takes an afternoon.** The second and third are the ones that hold up in a meeting.

## How the course is organised

**The course has seven modules, each built around something you can do at the end of it.**

| Module | What it gets you |
|---|---|
| **[0. How to use this course](m0-start-here.qmd)** | The capstone stated up front, a self-assessment, and the path that fits your background |
| **[1. What Q-CRAFT does and why it exists](m1-how-qcraft-thinks.qmd)** | A full projection in ten minutes, and the map: three numbers, one equation |
| **[2. The model, in three steps](m2-debt-equation.qmd)** | An equation, a growth engine, a climate overlay: the whole tool, traceable end to end |
| **[3. Choosing the parameters](m3-parameters.qmd)** | Every parameter set and defended, with the rationale written down |
| **[4. A worked example, end to end](m4-worked-example.qmd)** | One country from assumptions to a fiscal risk paragraph, then two more with less help |
| **[5. What the tool tells you and where it stops](m5-boundaries.qmd)** | The strengths, the documented exclusions, and which questions belong to a different tool |
| **[6. The capstone](m6-capstone.qmd)** | The capstone brief and rubric, and a look back at where you started |

**The tool covers most of the world, so the examples move country by country and the mechanism picks the country.** Demography reads clearest in a country whose workforce is already shrinking, set against one still growing fast. Productivity convergence reads clearest in an economy catching up to the frontier. The climate channel reads clearest where exposure is high. Module 4 runs one country, Uganda, the whole way through, because it is the tool's [golden-master](glossary.qmd#gloss-golden-master) verification country and every walkthrough figure can be checked against published documents. The exercises after it run on other countries, and the capstone runs on yours.

**Start at [Module 0](m0-start-here.qmd).** It takes about ten minutes and tells you which parts of the later modules you can read quickly. Module 2 is the spine: it assembles the whole tool in three steps, and everything after it either chooses the inputs, runs the thing or reads the output.

**The [Glossary](glossary.qmd) defines key terms and the [References](references.qmd) section annotates the primary sources behind the methodology.**

**Two appendices sit outside the learning path.** [Running the official workbook](appendix-workbook.qmd) is the quick orientation to the Excel half of the both-ways promise. The [appendix on co-design and the SovTech vision](appendix-codesign.qmd) is about the project behind the tool rather than about using it; read it to shape what the next version does.

## What this course defers to

**This is an educational companion to the IMF's User Guide [(Tim and Rahman, 2024)](references.qmd#src-user-guide), which remains the authoritative methodology reference, and to the IMF's own training materials, which remain the authoritative teaching materials.** Where this guide explains a concept, it cites the relevant User Guide section so you can go deeper. Where the two ever differ, the User Guide is right.

## The official materials

**The official sources are one click away throughout.**

- The IMF's [Q-CRAFT page](https://www.imf.org/en/Topics/fiscal-policies/Fiscal-Risks/Fiscal-Risks-Toolkit/Fiscal-Risks-Toolkit-Q-Craft), which posts the [User Guide (PDF)](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/topics/fiscal/fiscal-risks/tool/qcraft-user-guidev10.pdf) and the [Excel workbook](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/topics/fiscal/fiscal-risks/tool/qcraft-toolv10.xlsx) itself
- The climate methodology: [Kahn et al. (2021)](references.qmd#src-kahn-2021), and [IMF How-To Note 2025/009](references.qmd#src-imf-2025-howto), the public documentation of the FADCP Climate Dataset
- The published worked case: the [Uganda PFM Climate Assessment summary](references.qmd#src-imf-2024-uganda) (IMF, 2024) and [Uganda's Fiscal Risk Statement FY 2024/25](references.qmd#src-mofped-2024) (MoFPED, 2024)
- The data: the [IMF World Economic Outlook Database](references.qmd#src-weo) and the [UN World Population Prospects](references.qmd#src-unwpp)
- The wider assessment framework: the [C-PIMA Handbook](references.qmd#src-imf-2025-cpima) (IMF, 2025)

**Each entry on the [References](references.qmd) page carries a note on what the source is and how this course uses it.**

## Colophon

**This course is permissively licensed open source, free to use, copy and improve, and it builds completely from its repository.** It sets in Inter, IBM Plex Serif and IBM Plex Mono, three faces under the SIL Open Font License, bundled with the book rather than fetched from a font service. Clone the repository, run `quarto render docs/companion-guide`, and you get this book in the same three faces on a machine with no network access. Opening a page fetches no font from anyone's server, which matters in a ministry network that blocks outside hosts.

**Teal Insights also publishes a house edition of the same content, set in Klim Type Foundry faces where the license permits.** Those font files are not in the repository, because their license covers tealinsights.com. Where they are absent, every font stack falls through to the open faces and the book still sets. No word, number or figure in the course depends on which edition you are reading.

**The figures are built from the repository too.** `scripts/build_course_map.py` draws the course map that opens every module, `scripts/build_preface_figures.py` draws the two figures in this preface, and `scripts/build_parameter_context.py` draws the source-data figures in @sec-m3 from the same Parquet files the Explorer runs on. The screenshots are real captures: `scripts/build_app_screenshots.py` shoots the Explorer for the modules, and `scripts/capture_both_ways_shots.py` shoots the preface pair and the workbook appendix from the live deployment and the posted v10 workbook file.
